comments.body: @bernharddickore I think it was a wild solitary plant and not sown. It was located quite far from local settlements (the location provided in the map isn't the exact location).

@fungtr to my knowledge there isn’t anything comparable, persistently wild in the area. It isn’t Atriplex hortensis, which is likewise cultivated as an annual for greens. While probably at a lower scale than the lowlands, Ladakh and surroundings have a bunch of cultivated, useful or ornamental alien species, many of which documented here on inat, mostly without indication of floristic status. There is a lot of vegetative detritus around on your photo, which might indicate some lost or distributed supply of food or forage, or some favorable deposition spot for such, by high winds. All the caravan, transport and trekking routes may have these kind of at least temporary aliens, usually only somewhat diminishing at extreme altitudes

results.occurrenceRemarks: Identified as Royle's Pika by our guide. Since I cannot tell the differences to other Pika species, I would like to receive your feedback on the ID, thank you!

A flock of unknown finches, giving me a hard time for ID. I was not able to identify a solution so far. Any help from your side is greatly appreciated. Prominent features: black outer wings, forming a distinct bar on the side of the sitting birds. And a very thick and short bill, which on some of the pictures appears to be very light.

Rosefinch sp. in Rumbak, Ladakh, 4000m altitude. My best guess would be Streaked Rosefinch Carpodacus rubicilloides. Is Great Rosefinch C. rubicilla also possible? Your help with ID is greatly appreciated.

results.description: Edible (even raw) plant (as per one local). The colour of the leaves closely matched the colour of the surrounding rocks, which made it difficult to spot. Not sure if this is a property of the plant!

comments.body: @bernharddickore I think it was a wild solitary plant and not sown. It was located quite far from local settlements (the location provided in the map isn't the exact location).

@fungtr to my knowledge there isn’t anything comparable, persistently wild in the area. It isn’t Atriplex hortensis, which is likewise cultivated as an annual for greens. While probably at a lower scale than the lowlands, Ladakh and surroundings have a bunch of cultivated, useful or ornamental alien species, many of which documented here on inat, mostly without indication of floristic status. There is a lot of vegetative detritus around on your photo, which might indicate some lost or distributed supply of food or forage, or some favorable deposition spot for such, by high winds. All the caravan, transport and trekking routes may have these kind of at least temporary aliens, usually only somewhat diminishing at extreme altitudes
